concepts.topicTitle: Democratic Necessity of Periodic Elections and Electoral Representation
concepts.label: Why Elections Matter: Periodic, Direct and Indirect Elections
concepts.cardText: Elections are one of the most important processes for exercising democratic rights, and regular, periodic elections lie at the core of democracy. Representatives can be chosen through direct or indirect elections. In India, members of the Lok Sabha, the Vidhan Sabha and local bodies are elected directly every five years, while the President, Vice President and members of the Rajya Sabha are elected indirectly. Direct elections are those in which citizens vote directly to choose their leaders; indirect elections are those in which citizens vote for representatives who then elect the leaders. A government cannot continue beyond its term without seeking the people's mandate again, and we cannot exercise a choice if only one party contests. Elected representatives are accountable to the people: the right to elect them and hold them accountable is ensured through periodic elections, and our vote is the principal means. Elections give representation, accountability, legitimacy and equality.

concepts.topicTitle: Electoral Systems, Constituency Delimitation and Legal Frameworks
concepts.label: Electoral Systems: First-Past-The-Post and Proportional Representation
concepts.cardText: The first step in conducting elections is deciding how to convert votes cast into seats; the way an electoral system allocates seats distinguishes it from others. The framers of our Constitution chose the plurality system, known as First-Past-The-Post (FPTP): each voter votes for one candidate in a constituency and the candidate with the most votes wins, even with less than 50 per cent of votes polled. We elect the Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha by FPTP. The Rajya Sabha, the President and the Vice President are elected using proportional representation, in which voters vote for a party and seats are allotted in proportion to the votes each party gets, sharing power proportionately. Six states (Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh) have a bicameral legislature with a Vidhan Parishad elected by proportional representation by the single transferable vote.

concepts.topicTitle: Electoral Systems, Constituency Delimitation and Legal Frameworks
concepts.label: The Laws That Govern Elections: Representation of the People Acts
concepts.cardText: The major laws governing elections in India are the Representation of the People Act, 1950 (RPA 1950) and the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA 1951); there is also the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952. RPA 1950 deals mainly with the allocation of seats and delimitation of constituencies, the preparation and revision of electoral rolls, and ensuring that every citizen above 18 has the right to vote without discrimination. RPA 1951 deals with all other aspects of the conduct of elections and post-election disputes, laying down rules for nomination of candidates, election campaigns, voting procedures and dispute resolution. Together they ensure integrity, transparency and accountability. RPA 1951 also lists electoral offences and corrupt practices, such as gifts or promises to influence voting, appeals to vote on the basis of religion, caste, race, community or language, and taking help from government personnel.

concepts.topicTitle: Electoral Systems, Constituency Delimitation and Legal Frameworks
concepts.label: Delimitation of Constituencies
concepts.cardText: The boundaries of parliamentary and assembly constituencies are not permanently fixed; they change over time depending on shifts in population density. Without delimitation, one Member of Parliament might represent five lakh people while another represents twenty-five lakh, defeating the objective of equal representation. Delimitation is the process of determining the number of seats and fixing the territorial boundaries in each state for elections to the Lok Sabha and the Vidhan Sabha. It aims to make the ratio of seats to population as close to equal as possible across all constituencies. Article 82 of the Constitution mandates the establishment of a Delimitation Commission, and India has had four, in 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002.

concepts.topicTitle: Autonomous Election Machinery and Inclusive Voter Participation
concepts.label: The Election Commission of India: Structure and Functions
concepts.cardText: The Constitution vests in the Election Commission of India (ECI) the superintendence, direction and control of the entire process of conducting elections. The ECI is an autonomous permanent constitutional body established on 25 January 1950, which conducts elections to the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, Vidhan Sabha, Vidhan Parishad, President and Vice President; Articles 324 to 329 define its powers and duties. At the State level the Chief Electoral Officer supervises election work, and officers like District Magistrates act as District Election Officers and Returning Officers. Its functions include creating the electoral roll, with enumerators visiting every household and a Special Intensive Revision (SIR) to ensure no eligible citizen is left out and no ineligible person included; deciding the schedule, considering weather, agricultural cycle, examinations and festivals; and registering political parties and allocating symbols, ensuring inner-party democracy and acting as a quasi-judicial body in disputes.

concepts.topicTitle: Autonomous Election Machinery and Inclusive Voter Participation
concepts.label: Ensuring Free, Fair and Inclusive Elections
concepts.cardText: For elections to be meaningful, the entire process must be conducted in a fair and transparent manner: if fairness is not ensured, public confidence weakens. If candidates are influenced by personal favours, votes are not counted accurately, or some participants cannot vote because of accessibility problems, the democratic value of elections is reduced. Democracy is not only about conducting elections but also about making the process inclusive, impartial and trustworthy. The ECI has taken initiatives for infrastructure accessibility and technology-assisted inclusion for Persons with Disabilities, senior citizens, transgender persons and Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups: voting from home for senior citizens above 85 and PwDs with 40% benchmark disability was extended across India for the first time in the 2024 General Elections, and EVMs with Braille exist. Its digital ecosystem includes the Voter Helpline App, Saksham, cVIGIL for reporting violations, Suvidha, Sugam, ERONET and ETPBS. The ECI manages the exercise for over 96.8 crore voters autonomously with extensive use of technology and e-governance.

concepts.topicTitle: Political Party Dynamics, Alliances and Challenges to Free and Fair Elections
concepts.label: Political Parties and the Multi-Party System
concepts.cardText: There are often dozens of contestants for each constituency; most belong to a political party, though some contest independently. Voters learn about candidates, their policies and vision primarily through political parties. Parties organise public opinion, campaign on specific issues, offer voters meaningful choices and enable informed decisions. They are essential to a democratic system, working directly at the grassroots, and help democracy function effectively by providing governance, accountability, representation and public engagement. They present their agenda and promises at rallies and debate issues through the media. India has a multi-party system, reflecting its diversity of languages, cultures, religions and regions. The winning party forms the government and the opposition ensures accountability. The ECI classifies parties as recognised national or state parties or registered-unrecognised parties, using criteria such as share of valid votes and seats won.

concepts.topicTitle: Political Party Dynamics, Alliances and Challenges to Free and Fair Elections
concepts.label: Defection and the Anti-Defection Law
concepts.cardText: Once a person has been elected on a particular party's ticket, leaving that party is considered defection: abandoning or switching from the political party under whose banner the candidate was elected, whether joining another party or acting independently of the party's decisions, particularly in voting in the legislature. This can be seen as political opportunism when understood in the context of party discipline and political stability, though it can also be viewed as upholding conscience or responding to changing public expectations. The Anti-Defection Law was passed in 1985 through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, to prevent defection and give stability to the elected government. If a member of Parliament or a State Assembly voluntarily gives up party membership or votes against the party's instructions (whip), the member can be disqualified from the House, and the Speaker or Chairman decides.

concepts.topicTitle: Political Party Dynamics, Alliances and Challenges to Free and Fair Elections
concepts.label: Alliances and Challenges to Free and Fair Elections
concepts.cardText: The year 1967 ended the era of single-party dominated elections in India and began an era of alliances. In 1977, against the backdrop of the National Emergency, various parties formed the Janata Party alliance, which formed the first coalition government at the national level. Since the late 1990s the National Democratic Alliance (NDA), led by the BJP, and the United Progressive Alliance (UPA), led by the Indian National Congress until its dissolution in 2023 and reconstitution as the Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance, have been the major alliances. Conducting elections for over 96.8 crore voters with thousands of polling stations and hundreds of parties across diverse regions is challenging. Challenges include misinformation, fake news and intimidation, which the ECI addresses through the RPA 1950 and 1951, the Model Code of Conduct, EVMs, the Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT), voters' awareness campaigns and other measures. With constant vigilance and active citizen participation elections become more representative and democracy more robust.
